A browser tool that puts every carousel photo on the same white mat, like a gallery print
Instagram Carousel Tools with four autumn photos padded onto a shared 4:5 canvas

I use Instagram to post pictures from my hikes and trips, and nearly every one is nature or scenery. I like posting four or five at once as a carousel, but those photos come out in different aspect ratios. A wide mountain view sits next to a tall shot of a tree, and I wanted the whole set to look good when someone swipes through it in the app.
I wanted every slide on the same white canvas with a border around the photo, like a print in a gallery frame.
So I made a page for it: an
. You drop images in, it pads each one onto a shared canvas, and you download the result. Everything runs in your browser, so your photos are never uploaded.
Why I don't use Instagram's Mixed option

option in the crop menu that keeps each photo's own aspect ratio. The space around the wide photos isn't necessarily white, because Instagram fills it with a background that follows the app's theme. I can't control that background or how much space each photo gets, and I'd rather have white, which looks better to me.
Padding one wide photo and three tall ones to 4:5

I tested it with four photos from a walk in November: one wide 4:3 photo and three 4:5 tall ones. The page picked a 4:5 canvas of 1440 × 1800 pixels. The wide photo got white space above and below, and the tall ones got a thin border.
Instagram Carousel Tools showing four autumn photos on identical white canvases, the first one wide, with white space above and below
The first photo is the wide one. The slides share one canvas size.

The padding slider goes from 0 to 20%. Around 10% it starts to look matted. The ratio defaults to Auto, which picks the best fit for the set, and I can force 4:5, 1:1 or 1.91:1 instead. A click on any slide opens a swipe preview, and the padding slider stays in reach.
Preview viewer showing the wide autumn photo centered on a white 4:5 slide with navigation arrows and dots

I export at 1080 wide as JPEG, and the tool gives me a ZIP. It also supports 1440 wide and PNG. It stops at 20 slides, which is Instagram's cap, and warns when a file goes above 8 MB. My test photos came out between 670 KB and 1 MB each.
The layout math and canvas drawing behind the tool
The tool is a Nuxt page with a few Vue components and two small TypeScript files. One does the layout math and the other draws onto a

is an HTML element that gives you a blank grid of pixels that JavaScript can paint into. I picked it because the browser already does the hard parts: it decodes the photos, resizes them with smoothing when you draw them, and encodes the result as JPEG or PNG through
. So the tool doesn't need an image library or a server, which is why nothing gets uploaded. The previews on the page are canvases too, painted by the same code.

Scoring a few candidates instead of every ratio
The point of the tool is that every slide shares one canvas, so Auto mode needs one ratio for the whole set. A photo with ratio
of it. The total over all photos can only peak at one of the photos' own ratios or at a range limit, so the tool only scores those.
For my test set, 4:5 scores 3.6 (the three tall photos fill 100% of it, the wide one 60%) and 4:3 scores 2.8.
Because every photo fits into the same box, photos with the same aspect ratio end up in the same spot, even if one is 6000 pixels wide and the other 2000.

Rounding was the fiddly part. The code rounds one side of the canvas up so it's never too small for the photos. But JavaScript can't store most fractions exactly, so a value that should be whole sometimes comes out a hair above it. For an 878 × 800 photo with no padding, the height works out to
. Rounding that up gives 801, so the canvas is one pixel taller than the photo and a half-pixel strip of white shows along the top and bottom edges.
before rounding up. That's far bigger than the floating-point error and far smaller than any real fraction of a pixel, so the height comes out as 800.
